cb320557-3e95-4758-a395-588405337a43.implications: For a repo/financing desk this is mostly background on private-credit and structured-credit stress rather than a money-market catalyst, but the bank bridge-to-bond-market financing for the $22bn AI chip deal and insurer affiliated-loan cleanups are worth tracking as potential sources of primary IG issuance and collateral/counterparty risk; rising PIK usage and stressed maturity extensions are useful early-warning signals for CLO/leveraged-loan collateral quality.
key_claims: Fitch: trailing-12-month private credit default rate across 1,300 US borrowers rose to 6.3% in August, a new record
Fitch: stressed maturity extensions accounted for 45% of August defaults, the largest category for a third straight month
Houlihan Lokey: 11.8% of loans by size elected some PIK interest in Q2, representing 6.3% of total interest dollars

Houlihan Lokey: loans to $10-20mm EBITDA borrowers trading below 90 cents on the dollar rose from ~1% in 2023 to 12% now; $20-100mm EBITDA borrowers at 6% (three-year high); >$100mm EBITDA borrowers at 3%
Fitch: healthcare and industrial manufacturing each recorded a 9.9% default rate in August, the most stressed sectors; software default rate fell from 1.2% in July to 0.6% in August
Blackstone's BPP real estate fund has roughly $11bn NAV and is facilitating secondary sales amid redemption pressure
TWG-controlled insurers Delaware Life and Clear Spring disclosed over $20bn of loans/investments that should have been classified as affiliated but weren't

cb320557-3e95-4758-a395-588405337a43.one_liner: Fitch's record 6.3% private-credit default rate is largely a maturity-extension/liquidity story, not a wave of outright defaults, but it's spilling into real-estate fund redemptions, insurance-company affiliated-loan scrutiny (Mark Walter/TWG), and a $22bn bank bridge loan for an AI chip deal awaiting bond-market takeout.
cb320557-3e95-4758-a395-588405337a43.recap: The piece argues private credit's record 6.3% trailing-12-month default rate (Fitch, 1,300 US borrowers, August) understates the real story: 45% of August defaults were stressed maturity extensions, not missed payments, meaning lenders roll loans because borrowers can't refinance or sell. That traps lender cash — sometimes converted to payment-in-kind interest (Houlihan Lokey: 11.8% of loans by size took some PIK in Q2, 6.3% of interest dollars) — so reported income diverges from cash income. Floating-rate exposure plus sticky Fed policy squeezes highly leveraged borrowers' thin interest coverage. The stress is worst among smaller borrowers: loans to $10-20mm EBITDA companies trading below 90 cents on the dollar rose from ~1% in 2023 to 12% now; $20-100mm EBITDA borrowers hit 6% (three-year high); >$100mm borrowers only 3%. Healthcare and industrial manufacturing led sector defaults at 9.9%; software defaults fell to 0.6% but valuations face AI-disruption risk. The same liquidity crunch shows up elsewhere: Blackstone and Invesco face redemption pressure and are arranging secondary sales/fee cuts in open-ended real estate funds (Blackstone's BPP fund, ~$11bn NAV); Mark Walter's TWG-controlled insurers (Delaware Life, Clear Spring) disclosed over $20bn of previously misclassified affiliated loans amid regulatory scrutiny, prompting Walter to sell the LA Lakers and explore selling Chelsea stakes; and ten banks are bridging a $22bn loan for Blackstone/Alphabet's Crux AI Google-TPU venture, intended to later be refinanced in the IG bond market. SoftBank's 5-year CDS hit its highest level since 2023 on OpenAI-related exposure concerns. The author frames all this as capital being rationed rather than disappearing.
terms: PIK -- payment-in-kind, where interest accrues to loan principal instead of being paid in cash
CDS -- credit default swap, a derivative providing protection against a borrower's default
EBITDA -- earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization
